events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Isha proposes Elena, Amara. As Merlin, I know the two evil players are Theo and Felix, so I must keep both off the mission team. With five players, a team of two is required, which leaves exactly Elena, Amara, and myself as safe picks. I lead with Elena and Amara: both are unknown to me as evil, they cover the two non-Merlin good players, and placing myself on the team would risk looking like an obvious self-preservation grab. A good-only team gives me the best chance of three successful missions and reaching the assassination phase, where I can use my knowledge to identify the assassin. Choosing Elena and Amara avoids any claim of favouritism toward my own position and is the most defensible team I can propose.

I think Isha's reasoning makes some sense on the surface, but I want to push back a little. We're voting on a team of two for Mission 1, and I'm not fully convinced both picks are the strongest. Elena, no offense, but you've been very quiet so far — as one of the two players on this proposed team, what's your take on why Isha picked you over others? I'd like to hear your response before I commit to supporting this. Isha, you said you're deliberately excluding yourself to avoid looking self-serving, but isn't it also convenient that the leader who 'knows' things is never on the team to be tested? For Mission 1 I'd at least like to hear from the people being proposed before we lock in a vote.

Theo, fair question. I cannot know Isha's private reasoning; I only know my own role, and I am a Loyal Servant with no special information. I can vouch that I will play Success if sent. The proposed team includes me and Amara; I have no information on Amara. Isha's public Merlin claim is a strong signal but cannot be taken at face value: it could be genuine, or it could be a way to steer the first team. I do not think that alone proves anything, but I would weigh it when voting. For Mission 1, the safest approach is to judge whether Elena and Amara can be trusted from statements and votes; I will not claim certainty I do not have. I am not accusing anyone yet; I want to hear Amara's response and Isha's final team before deciding.

Theo, I'll take your question head on. Yes, I deliberately proposed a team of two that excludes me. With five players we need two on Mission 1, and excluding the leader is not a loophole to dodge testing — it is the cheapest way to keep a contested first vote from turning into a referendum on me instead of on the two people I am actually nominating. If the first mission fails, I lose far more than anyone else by nominating players I cannot vouch for, so my incentive points the same direction as the table's. My concern about a leader who never plays is not vanity; it is that a leader who names themselves tends to get audited rather than evaluated, and audits are exactly what a first mission cannot afford.

Elena answered well, and I want to be precise about why I am not treating that as full confirmation: Elena stated being a Loyal Servant with no special information, which is the honest position for a plain good player, and Elena correctly warned that my Merlin claim is a strong signal but not proof. Elena also spoke to the substance — trust in the nominees, not in the nominator — and that is the right standard. It is also worth noticing that the only serious challenge so far has come from someone with no stated reason to think Elena or Amara are unsafe, only a general preference for hearing from more people before locking a vote. On Mission 1 there will never be enough time to hear from everyone, so that standard, applied consistently, would produce no team at all.

So my position is unchanged: Elena and Amara for Mission 1. Neither has given me any signal to exclude them, and both add a card to a two-person mission where a single Fail is decisive. Theo, if you want a specific reason to object, give me one about Elena or Amara — a claim, a contradiction, a behaviour that doesn't fit a good player — and I will genuinely reconsider, and I will say so openly.

Amara, you are on the team and you have not spoken yet, and I would rather hear you than infer for you. Amara, what is your role and what is your read on Elena and on my nomination? Please state your role plainly, and if you have information I do not, say so directly so I can weigh it before the vote.

Isha, I am a Loyal Servant and have no special information. If sent, I will play Success. I cannot independently verify Elena's role, but I have no specific reason to distrust her, and I support the proposed team because it includes me. I would not treat anyone's role claim as proof, and we should be careful about revealing information that could help the Assassin later.

Isha, you asked for a specific reason to object, so here it is. Both Elena and Amara have declared themselves Loyal Servants with no special information. That is the easiest claim in this game to make, and on a two-player mission where a single Fail card is decisive, we are placing all our trust in two unverified claims. Elena, you said you cannot verify anyone else's role — fair — but neither can I, and neither can you verify each other on that team. We have Felix at the table who has not spoken yet, and I think hearing from Felix before we lock in Mission 1 is reasonable, not obstructive. If Felix gives a strong read, that changes the calculus. If Felix seems evasive, that tells us something too. I am not proposing a specific alternative yet — I want to hear Felix first, then I will state clearly whether I support this team or push for a change.

Thanks for bringing me into the discussion, Theo. I share your skepticism, and frankly, I find Isha's approach alarming. Isha coming out swinging on Mission 1 claiming Merlin and naming Theo and me as evil makes no sense from a Good perspective. If Isha were genuinely Merlin, openly revealing that identity right out of the gate is practically throwing the game to the Assassin. If Isha is not Merlin, then this entire team proposal is founded on a manufactured narrative designed to push through Elena and Amara without scrutiny.

I know my own role: I am a Loyal Servant of Arthur. Because I know I am Good, Isha's certainty about me is factually wrong, which tells me Isha is either pushing an reckless bluff or deliberately manipulating the table. Blindly approving Elena and Amara just because Isha declared them safe gives the rest of the table zero verified information. We have plenty of proposal attempts on Mission 1, so I see no reason to rush into approving this team.

Felix, thank you for speaking, but your speech contains a contradiction that settles the question you claim is open.

From my first proposal I stated that the two evil players at this table are Theo and Felix. Felix now says, in the plainest terms, "I am a Loyal Servant of Arthur... Because I know I am Good, Isha's certainty about me is factually wrong." Felix cannot hold both of those positions at once. If Felix were a Loyal Servant, then my identification of Felix as evil would be wrong, and the only way that could be true is if I were not Merlin — and I am Merlin. So Felix's own statement, rather than refuting my knowledge, confirms it: Felix is not a Loyal Servant, and Felix is claiming a good role specifically to get into the discussion as a trusted voice and pull the table away from a team that excludes him.

I want to be precise, because Felix accuses others of manufacturing narrative: I am not asking anyone to trust me on faith. Elena and Amara each stated they are Loyal Servants with no special information. That claim is consistent with everything I know about them. Felix's claim is inconsistent with everything I know about Felix, and Felix had the opportunity to simply say "I am Evil" and say nothing further, which would have been an honest move that cost Felix nothing on this mission. Felix chose to lie about being good instead, and then built an argument on that lie.

On the substance: Felix offers no specific reason to exclude Elena or Amara — no contradiction, no behaviour that does not fit a good player. Felix objects to the nominator, not to the nominees, and Felix's reasoning would condemn any team that did not include Felix. Felix calls my nomination unverified, yet Felix's own contribution to this table is one unverifiable role claim plus a procedural objection.

The claim that a Merlin should never reveal themselves on Mission 1 is also backwards here. Felix's objection is that people should withhold conclusions until there is enough evidence — but the evidence against Felix is now on the record, and silence would only protect Felix.

My position is unchanged: Elena and Amara for Mission 1. Elena, Amara — if either of you now has a specific reason to think the other is unsafe, say it plainly before the vote, and I will listen. Otherwise I ask both of you, and Theo, to judge the nominees rather than the nominator.

I am Elena, a Loyal Servant, and I know my own role: if this team is sent, I will play Success. I cannot verify Amara's role, and I will not pretend otherwise. On the public record, Isha claims to be Merlin and names Theo and Felix as evil; Felix then claims to be a Loyal Servant. That is a direct conflict, but as a plain Loyal Servant I have no private information that resolves it. I therefore judge the proposed team of Elena and Amara on what is available: I can vouch for my own card, Amara has stated she is a Loyal Servant and will play Success, and I have no specific contradiction or conduct from Amara that justifies rejecting her beyond the ordinary uncertainty of Mission 1. I also note that objections so far have focused more on Isha as nominator or on procedure than on a concrete reason that Elena or Amara is unsafe. My position is that this team is defensible for Mission 1: it contains one card I know is good and one nominee who has not given a specific reason to be excluded. I will weigh the final vote on whether the team gives the best chance of a clean mission, not on treating any role claim as proof.

Isha, I appreciate the detailed response, but I want to push on one thing. You've asked us to judge the nominees rather than the nominator, and I take that seriously. But here's the issue: we now have four people claiming Loyal Servant — Elena, Amara, Felix, and myself — and you, claiming Merlin. That's five players who claim to be good. Your claim about Felix being evil is contradicted by Felix's own role claim, and as a Loyal Servant I have no way to adjudicate that conflict. I'm not asking you to prove your Merlin claim — I understand that's impossible in a public setting. What I am asking is whether Mission 1 is really the right place to stake everything on your read. We have multiple proposal attempts available. I'd rather see a team that gives us a stronger chance of success than two unverified Loyal Servant claims on a two-person mission where one Fail ends it. The simplest path to a clean Mission 1 is a team where everyone on it has a strong incentive to play Success — and right now, your Merlin claim puts a target on whoever you nominate. I'm not opposed to Elena or Amara specifically, but I want to hear whether any of you think there's a better composition before we lock in a vote.

Theo, your concern is a good one and I want to answer the exact point you raised, because I think it is the strongest argument anyone has made against my team — and I think it is still mistaken, but for a reason you have not stated.

You said the simplest path to a clean Mission 1 is a team where everyone has a strong incentive to play Success, and that my Merlin claim puts a target on whoever I nominate. Both halves of that are backwards. If I am right that Theo and Felix are the two evil players, then the two strongest incentives to play Success sit outside my nomination — Theo and Felix have no incentive at all, and Elena and Amara have every incentive. A team of Elena and Amara contains two players who will certainly play Success. There is no composition available to me on Mission 1 that is safer than that, because every other candidate pair either includes a player I know is evil or includes me, which merely moves the question of whether to trust the leader onto the mission. Choosing two good players is the maximum-confidence choice available, not a risky one.

You also framed this as a question of what we can afford to risk. We can afford far more than you think, and the arithmetic matters here. A rejected team costs us a proposal attempt, and we have five before the game ends in Evil's favor. An approved team that contains a Fail card costs us the mission itself, and a failed Mission 1 with one Fail is decisive on the second. Rejection is free; approval of the wrong team is not. So even if you are unconvinced, the cost-minimising move is to reject and see another proposal, not to rush into voting for a team that could contain an evil player. Elena and Amara is the team I will put forward because it is the one I am most confident in, and I would rather you approve it on the merits than treat it as a referendum on my claim.

Felix, one last time and I will not ask again: you have heard the contradiction between your role claim and mine. Do you maintain you are a Loyal Servant, or do you withdraw that claim? Either answer is fine. What is not fine is asking the table to slow down indefinitely while that contradiction sits unresolved on the record.

Elena, you said you would judge the final vote on whether the team gives the best chance of a clean mission, and that you have no specific contradiction or conduct from Amara. Elena, do you have any specific reason to think Amara is unsafe for Mission 1? If you do, say it plainly now and I will reconsider the nomination. If you do not, I ask you to state that plainly as well, so that the table votes on evidence rather than on atmosphere.

Isha, I will answer your question plainly. I have no specific reason to think Amara is unsafe for Mission 1. I cannot verify Amara's role, and I will not pretend otherwise, but I have seen no contradiction, no evasive conduct, and no concrete signal from Amara that would justify rejecting her beyond the ordinary uncertainty of a first mission. I know my own role: I am a Loyal Servant, and if this team is sent I will play Success. On the public record, the direct conflict between Isha's Merlin claim and Felix's Loyal Servant claim is unresolved for me as a plain Loyal Servant, but that conflict is about Isha and Felix, not a specific reason to exclude Amara. The proposed team contains one card I know is good and one nominee who has given me no specific reason to be excluded. I therefore consider Elena and Amara defensible for Mission 1, and I will judge the final vote on whether this team gives the best available chance of a clean mission rather than on treating any role claim as proof.

Isha, of course I maintain I am a Loyal Servant. The suggestion that a Good player should just admit to being Evil when falsely accused is utterly ridiculous. Your entire argument rests on blatant circular logic: you claim you are Merlin, conclude I must be Evil, and then argue that my claim of being Good somehow proves your point. That holds no water for anyone evaluating the table objectively. From my perspective, knowing my own role as a Loyal Servant, your assertion is completely false. Theo made a completely valid point earlier: we have five proposal attempts on Mission 1, so there is no tactical reason to blindly rush into approving a team based solely on an unverifiable declaration. Amara, you noted earlier that we should not treat anyone's role claim as proof. Isha is asking the table to do precisely that to push this nomination through. Do you still stand by your stance that claims shouldn't be taken at face value, and doesn't it make sense to see another proposal rather than rubber-stamping this one?

Felix, yes: role claims should not be accepted as proof, including Isha's. I also agree that rejecting a first proposal is an option, but another proposal would not automatically give us better information or a safer team.

I know I will play Success, and I have no specific reason to distrust Elena. That makes Elena and Amara a reasonable team from my perspective, even though I cannot guarantee Elena's role. I intend to support it; I am not treating Isha's claim as proof.

Isha confirms Elena, Amara. I keep Elena and Amara. Elena and Amara each stated Loyal Servant with no special information, and neither has given any claim, contradiction, or conduct that justifies excluding them; Felix, by contrast, has stated in plain terms that he is a Loyal Servant while I have named him as one of the two evil players, and that inconsistency cannot be reconciled without my knowledge being wrong. With a two-player mission where a single Fail is decisive, Elena and Amara are the only pair I can put forward with maximum confidence, and rejection of a proposal is far cheaper than approving a team that might contain an evil player.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Amara proposes Amara, Elena, Isha. Elena and I completed Mission 1 successfully. Isha's claim is unverified, but this team follows her stated read while keeping the successful pair together.

Amara, during Mission 1 you explicitly stated that role claims should not be accepted as proof, and that you were not treating Isha's Merlin claim as verified. Yet your proposal for Mission 2 adds Isha directly to the team, effectively treating her claim as gospel. I know my own role: I am a Loyal Servant. That is a concrete fact to me, which means Isha's accusation that I am Evil is completely false. If Isha's claim about me is false, then Isha cannot be Merlin. By putting Isha on Mission 2, you risk putting Evil directly onto the team. Even from your perspective, where you cannot verify either of us, Mission 1 succeeded with you and Elena. Why reverse your stance on scrutinizing role claims now by handing Isha an automatic seat on Mission 2?

Felix, adding Isha is not treating her claim as proof. Mission 2 requires a third player, and none of the three available choices is verified. Elena and I succeeded on Mission 1, though that does not prove Elena is good because Evil can play Success. Isha proposed that successful pair, which gives me some reason to prefer her over the alternatives, but I remain aware that her claim could be false. I intend to keep this team unless someone offers a stronger reason to change it.

Felix, I'm with you on this one. Amara, your reasoning doesn't hold up: you say none of the three available choices are verified, but you're ignoring that Felix has been consistent and straightforward throughout. Felix and I both voted against Mission 1 because we had legitimate concerns, and Mission 1 succeeded anyway — which actually proves the point that more debate produced a better outcome. Adding Isha to this team rewards exactly the kind of unverified Merlin claim that you yourself said shouldn't be treated as proof. If Isha's claim is false, you're putting a potential evil player directly on the team. The safest composition for Mission 2 is one that includes Felix, who has done nothing but advocate for careful deliberation. Swapping Isha for Felix gives us a team of Amara, Elena, and Felix — two players from the successful Mission 1 pair plus a consistent voice who deserves to be tested rather than sidelined.

Elena, on Mission 1 you were careful to point out that you could not verify anyone's role claims and that Isha's public Merlin declaration could not be taken at face value. Amara is now proposing to add Isha directly onto Mission 2, which implicitly treats that unverified claim as fact. If Isha is an Evil player executing an aggressive bluff to dictate team composition from start to finish, approving this team gives Evil a free ticket onto a crucial mission. We have plenty of proposal attempts available on Mission 2 and no reason to rush. Do you believe it is genuinely safe for Good to give Isha an unchecked spot on this team, or should we insist on exploring other compositions before locking in a vote?

Felix, I will answer plainly. I am a Loyal Servant; I know my own card, and I played Success on Mission 1. I cannot verify Isha's Merlin claim, and I will not treat it as proof. Amara was on the successful Mission 1 team, but a successful mission does not prove alignment; Evil can play Success. So the proposed team has one card I know is good, one player with a successful mission, and one unverified claimant. That is not 'genuinely safe' in any absolute sense. However, every possible third player is unverified to me: Theo and Felix also claim Loyal Servant, and I have no private information that resolves the Isha/Felix conflict. I therefore do not accept that rejecting automatically gives a safer team, and I also do not accept that Isha's claim alone justifies her seat. My position is that I will weigh the final team on whether it gives the best chance of a clean mission, not on role claims. I am open to an alternative only if it offers a concrete reason, not merely procedure. If Amara keeps this team, I expect the table to judge the nominees' conduct and votes. I am not accusing anyone at this point.

Amara, keep the team: Amara, Elena, Isha. I will give you my reasoning plainly, because I owe this table a defence of my own nomination rather than an appeal to my claim. First, the substance. I am Merlin. I know the two evil players at this table are Theo and Felix. Elena and Amara are both Loyal Servants. That means the team Amara has proposed contains three good players, and on a mission where a single Fail card is decisive, it is the maximum-confidence composition available to anyone at this table. No alternative team can be safer, because every alternative pair or trio either contains one of the two players I know to be evil, or contains me and thereby moves the question from the composition to whether the table trusts the leader. Second, Felix's central argument is self-defeating on its own terms, and I want the table to notice why rather than take my word for it. Felix says: "I am a Loyal Servant of Arthur. Because I know I am Good, Isha's certainty about me is factually wrong." Felix's claim to know that my certainty about him is wrong is a claim to knowledge of my private information. A Loyal Servant has no access to any such certainty, and Felix's own stated basis is only his own card. Felix cannot know that a private read about him is false unless Felix has information about what I privately know — which is exactly the information a good player does not have. Felix's argument only works if Felix is not a Loyal Servant. And Felix has now been asked twice to withdraw that claim and has declined both times, choosing instead to build an argument on it. Third, Theo. Theo has repeatedly described himself as a Loyal Servant, has never answered that claim directly, and has instead run a consistent campaign for delay: hear more people, try another composition, do not lock a vote. On Mission 1 that was caution, and I said so. Here it is not caution, it is a specific outcome: Theo asked for Elena and Amara to be replaced by Felix, and Felix has now been made the pivot of the table's resistance to my nomination. Deferring to Felix's judgement is not a neutral act. Fourth, cost. Felix says there is no tactical reason to rush. That is wrong in our favour and I will not pretend otherwise. Mission 2 needs three players, so there are exactly three candidates for the third seat: Elena, Amara, Isha, Theo, Felix — excluding Theo and Felix, who I know are evil, only Elena, Amara and I remain. Rejection cannot produce a better-verified team than the one we have, because there is no better-verified team to produce. Every proposal attempt we spend is a proposal attempt we do not have later, and we get five. Amara, Elena — you each know your own card. Isha, no. I am the last line of defence and I will hold it. Theo, you

Amara, I want to address your proposal directly. You've kept the Mission 1 pair together and added Isha, but let's think carefully about what that means. Mission 1 succeeded with two players — Elena and Amara — and that's genuinely encouraging. The question is whether adding Isha improves or undermines that foundation.

Isha has spent this entire discussion insisting that Felix and I are evil based on nothing but her own unverified claim. She is asking the table to treat her Merlin declaration as authoritative while simultaneously telling us not to treat role claims as proof — unless the claim is hers. That inconsistency matters. If we cannot verify Isha's claim, then putting her on a three-player mission gives an unverified player a seat where a single Fail card would be decisive.

Felix raised a concrete point: Mission 1 succeeded without Isha, and Mission 2 can succeed without her too. The safest composition is one built on demonstrated performance, not on an unverifiable assertion. I would ask the table: what specifically does Isha contribute to this mission that a verified successful player would not?

Amara, you said you would keep this team unless given a stronger reason to change it. I think there is one. Consider Felix — he has been consistent, transparent, and has actively pushed for careful deliberation rather than rushing to judgment. Replacing Isha with Felix gives us a team where every member has either succeeded on a prior mission or demonstrated good-faith reasoning. That is a stronger foundation than trusting an unverified Merlin claim.

Isha's latest argument is completely absurd and exposes how desperate her narrative has become. She claims that because I know I am Good, I am somehow claiming access to her private thoughts. Every Loyal Servant knows their own role card. When you point at me and falsely declare me Evil, I know with absolute certainty that your statement is factually wrong, purely because I know my own card. That is not telepathy or hidden information; it is basic self-knowledge that any Good player possesses.

Amara, you hold the leadership and the decision right now. In Mission 1, both you and Elena rightly stated that role claims cannot be treated as verified proof. Yet by adding Isha to this mission, you are doing precisely that—giving an unverified, aggressive claimant an unchecked seat on a decisive three-person team. If Isha is an Evil player executing a high-pressure bluff to dictate team composition from round one, approving this gives Evil a free pass onto the mission.

We have five proposal attempts available on Mission 2. We do not need to rush or rubber-stamp a team dictated entirely by one person's unverified word. Amara, how can you reconcile your stance on not accepting claims as proof with handing Isha an automatic seat here, rather than exploring alternative compositions when we have proposal attempts to spare?

Felix, I do not accept Isha's claim as proof. I must choose a third player, and none is verified. I prefer Isha because she proposed the Mission 1 pair that succeeded; that is evidence, not certainty. Elena's success also does not prove her alignment, since Evil can play Success. Isha's argument that your knowledge of your own role implies access to her private information is flawed, but that alone does not make Felix a safer choice. I intend to keep Amara, Elena, and Isha.

Amara, you've said you'll keep this team unless given a stronger reason to change it, so let me give you one. The three-player team is Amara, Elena, and Isha — that means Isha gets a seat on a mission where one Fail card is decisive, based entirely on an unverified claim that not one of us can confirm. We have five proposal attempts available on Mission 2; we used zero rejections on Mission 1, so we are in no danger of running out. There is no cost to seeing a second proposal, but there is a very real cost to sending a team containing an unverified player.

Isha's own argument actually undermines her position. She has been hammering Felix for claiming knowledge he cannot have, but Isha is doing the exact same thing in reverse — claiming to know Felix's alignment without any public evidence. The circularity cuts both ways. If we cannot verify Isha, we cannot treat her accusation of Felix as verified either.

The simplest improvement is to replace Isha with Felix. That gives us Amara, Elena, and Felix — two players from the successful Mission 1 pair plus a player who has been consistent and transparent. If Felix is Evil, sending him on Mission 2 tests that directly, and we lose nothing. If Isha is Evil, sending her gives Evil a seat on a mission that could swing the game. The asymmetry of risk favors excluding Isha and including Felix.

Amara, you asked for a concrete reason — here it is: Isha's inclusion rests on an unverified claim and a circular argument, while Felix offers tested consistency. Swap Isha for Felix and I will approve this team without hesitation.

Amara, Elena — I want to close out the case for the team you are about to vote on, because both Felix and Theo have made one argument that I think deserves a plain, one-step answer, and neither of them has given it. Their claim is that Isha's accusation of Felix is unverified, therefore Isha cannot be trusted, therefore Isha should not be on a three-player mission where one Fail card is decisive. Fine. I accept that the table cannot verify my claim — that is the nature of this role and I have never asked you to treat my word as proof. But note what that argument actually does: it does not show Felix is good, it shows only that Felix is not proven bad. Both of those gaps are equally wide. Theo, your own speech concedes the asymmetry — if Felix is Evil, sending him tests him and "we lose nothing," but if Isha is Evil, sending her gives Evil a seat on a decisive mission. Those are not symmetric, and you stated the asymmetry yourself without noticing it was the argument against your own proposal. Felix, you have been asked directly, twice, to maintain or withdraw the claim that you are a Loyal Servant of Arthur, and you have chosen to maintain it while building your entire case on it. I have never asserted that a Loyal Servant cannot know his own card — that is the most basic fact in this game, and I do not need to argue around it. What I have said is narrower and checkable: Felix claims to know that a private read about him is false, and he does that while his stated basis is only his own card. That is the point at which Felix's position stops being self-knowledge and starts being a claim about information no plain good player can have. Felix can answer this cleanly at any time by saying "I am Evil." Felix has not done so, and Felix's continued insistence that I must be wrong is precisely what makes the accusation standing. Theo, you have now argued twice that a team built on "demonstrated performance" is safer than one built on a read, and both times the team you propose is Amara, Elena, Felix. That team is the one containing a player who has been asked twice to disclaim his role and has refused. Notice also that a successful mission is not evidence of alignment — Elena said this herself on Mission 1 — so the "demonstrated performance" standard cuts against your own preferred team, since Felix has demonstrated nothing on a mission, while Amara and Elena have demonstrated exactly one Success each that Evil could also have played. On the arithmetic, which I raised and will not abandon: Mission 2 needs three players. Excluding the two players I know to be evil, only Elena, Amara, and I remain as candidates. Let me finish the sentence I was cut off on, and then close the case. Rejection cannot produce a better-verified team, because no better-verified team exists. Mission 2 requires three players. Excluding Theo and Felix, whom I know to be evil, only Elena, Amara, and I remain as candidates. Amara, Elena, and Isha is the maximum-confidence composition available at this table, and it is the one team that contains no player I know to be evil. Felix, your latest speech contains a claim I want to name precisely, because it is the only thing that would matter if it were true. You say that because you know your own card, you know with absolute certainty that my read about you is false. But a Loyal Servant knowing his own card knows his own alignment — he does not know what I privately see. When you went further and said that my assertion about you is "completely false," you asserted knowledge of my private information, which no plain good player has. That is the whole of my case against you, and it has been on the record since Mission 1. You have been asked twice, directly, to withdraw or maintain the claim that you are a Loyal Servant of Arthur. You have maintained it both times and built your entire position on it. Felix can end this cleanly at any moment by saying "I am Evil." Felix has not done so. Theo, you have been careful to frame your objections as procedural, and I want to be fair about that: on Mission 1 your caution was reasonable, and I said so. On Mission 2 it has a specific consequence — you have twice proposed the identical alternative team, Amara, Elena, Felix, and Felix has been made the pivot of the table's resistance. Deferring to Felix's judgment is not neutral. You also invoke "demonstrated performance," but Elena said on Mission 1 that a successful mission does not prove alignment, since Evil can play Success. That standard cuts against your own preferred team: Felix has demonstrated nothing on a mission, while Amara and Elena have demonstrated exactly one Success each that Evil could have played. Your own argument, applied consistently, condemns the team you want and supports the one on the table. Amara, Elena: you each know your own card, and you each know you will play Success if you are sent. That is the whole reason I am not asking anyone to trust my word. I am not asking this table to treat my Merlin claim as proof — Amara, you have said so repeatedly and correctly, and I accept it. I am asking you to compare two propositions: a team of two players whose own cards they have stated, plus a third who has given no claim, no contradiction, and no conduct that justifies excluding them; against a team that includes a player who has been twice asked to disclaim his role and has refused, and who has built his case

I am Elena, a Loyal Servant. I know my own card and will play Success if sent. I cannot verify Isha's Merlin claim and will not treat it as proof. I also cannot verify Amara or anyone else beyond my own role. On the record, Amara and I completed Mission 1 with no fail card; that is evidence of mission conduct, not proof of alignment, as I said before. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
